title: Windows Server 2028 trades compatibility for out-of-the-box security
gist: At Ignite, Microsoft unveiled the Windows Server 2028 Public Preview, whose Server Core installs ship hardened by default to a DoD/DISA STIG-aligned baseline (Kerberos over NTLM, modern-only TLS, hybrid post-quantum ML-KEM key exchange) plus a default-on native NVMe stack. Microsoft openly warns the defaults may break legacy software, and the preview has a known LSASS crash bug in the hybrid TLS key exchange.

insights.claim: Windows Server 2028 Public Preview, revealed at Microsoft Ignite, ships a default security framework that Microsoft says is aligned with hardened DoD benchmarks such as DISA's Security Technical Implementation Guide (STIG).
insights.speaker: Nick Indge
insights.so_what: Default STIG alignment lowers compliance effort for government and regulated buyers and may shift work away from third-party hardening tools.

insights.claim: Microsoft shifts Windows Server from a blank-canvas model where admins hardened servers after setup to a model where the secure configuration is the starting state, closing the exposure window of newly deployed servers.
insights.speaker: Nick Indge
insights.so_what: Industry trend toward secure-by-default; reduces misconfiguration risk but transfers compatibility pain to deployment time.
insights.quote: The secure configuration is the starting state, not a project you run after setup.
insights.locator: STIGs work by providing a standard security framework

insights.claim: The hardened-by-default state applies only to Windows Server 2028 Server Core installs; Desktop Experience installs keep the old stance.
insights.speaker: Nick Indge
insights.so_what: Pushes enterprises toward headless Server Core deployments.
insights.locator: The new Windows Server 2028 hardened-by-default state

insights.claim: Windows Server 2028 makes Kerberos the default over NTLM with added LSASS protections, restricts TLS to modern cipher suites, uses hybrid post-quantum key exchange based on ML-KEM, and tightens remote desktop authentication and PowerShell script block logging.
insights.speaker: Nick Indge
insights.so_what: Post-quantum crypto entering default enterprise server builds marks mainstream PQC adoption.
insights.locator: Kerberos is now the default over NTLM

insights.claim: Microsoft's native NVMe storage stack, introduced as an opt-in update for Windows Server 2025, eliminates NVMe translation through a SCSI stack for faster speeds and lower overhead, and will be on by default in Windows Server 2028.
insights.speaker: Nick Indge
insights.so_what: Default native NVMe improves storage performance for Windows Server workloads.

insights.claim: Microsoft warns that Windows Server 2028's hardened defaults may break software relying on older protocols, legacy authentication, or management tools and scripts, and is soliciting feedback before general availability.
insights.speaker: Nick Indge
insights.so_what: Legacy-heavy enterprises face migration friction; watch for vendor compatibility updates ahead of GA.
insights.quote: We want to hear where a hardened default gets in the way of a real workload
insights.locator: Microsoft is upfront, noting that the new hardened

insights.claim: The Windows Server 2028 Public Preview is not a release candidate: Secure Boot and DMA hardware requirements and NTLM blocking will only arrive in later preview builds.
insights.speaker: Nick Indge
insights.so_what: Stricter hardware requirements are still coming and could drive server hardware refresh decisions.
insights.locator: Microsoft suggests that users use the preview build

insights.claim: The current Windows Server 2028 preview has a known race condition in the TLS hybrid key exchange that can crash LSASS, and Microsoft recommends disabling hybrid key exchange groups until it is fixed.
insights.speaker: Nick Indge
insights.so_what: Early post-quantum TLS implementations carry stability risk.
insights.quote: A race condition in the TLS hybrid key exchange implementation may cause the LSASS service to crash when hybrid groups are negotiated by a TLS server.

insights.claim: Microsoft is providing an MSHardenedPolicyEval scoring tool to evaluate hardened policy state, but cautions the tool is still being refined.
insights.speaker: Nick Indge
